hints: Look at the limewater result first, it is really a clever way to count how many carbon atoms are in one molecule of X.
Work out moles of CaCO3 from 3.0 g, this equals moles of CO2, then compare 0.03 mol CO2 from 0.0075 mol X to find carbons per molecule.
Use the dichromate test to decide the alcohol type, orange to green means oxidation has happened so X cannot be tertiary, then match carbon number with alcohol class.
walkthrough:
**Find moles of CO2 from the limewater precipitate**

Each mole of CO2 that bubbles through limewater makes one mole of CaCO3. So we can count CO2 by weighing the solid.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
$$n(\text{CaCO}_3) = \frac{3.0}{100} = 0.030 \text{ mol}$$
Therefore $n(\text{CO}_2) = 0.030 \text{ mol}$.

**Find number of carbons in one molecule of X**

Complete combustion turns every carbon in the alcohol into one CO2. Compare moles of X burnt with moles of CO2 made.

Calculation rule:
$$\text{carbons per molecule} = \frac{n(\text{CO}_2)}{n(\text{X})}$$
$$\text{carbons per molecule} = \frac{0.030}{0.0075} = 4$$
So X must be a $\text{C}_4$ alcohol.

**Use dichromate test to find alcohol class**

Orange $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ turning green $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ means the dichromate has oxidised the alcohol. Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised, tertiary alcohols are not.

This tells us X is primary or secondary, not tertiary. A $\text{C}_4$ secondary alcohol fits both clues perfectly.

options.A: CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 is butan-2-ol. It has 4 carbon atoms, so 1 mol gives 4 mol CO2, matching the 0.0075 to 0.030 ratio. It is a secondary alcohol, so it is oxidised by warm acidified dichromate(VI) and gives the orange to green change.
options.B: (CH3)3COH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. It does have 4 carbons, but it is a tertiary alcohol with no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the OH group. It resists oxidation, so no orange to green change would be seen.
options.C: CH3CH2CH2OH is propan-1-ol. It is primary so it would give the orange to green change, but it has only 3 carbons. 0.0075 mol would give only 0.0225 mol CO2, giving 2.25 g CaCO3, not 3.0 g.
options.D: CH3CH(OH)CH3 is propan-2-ol. It is secondary so it would give the orange to green change, but it has only 3 carbons. Like option C, it would produce too little CO2 and too little CaCO3.
